title: How to Build a Personal “Start Here” Page for the Web
content:
A personal “start here” page should help you begin a task without first searching through bookmarks, chat history, and forgotten tabs. It is a small map of useful destinations, not a second search engine and not a public directory of every site you have ever liked.

Start by listing the activities you repeat: open current work, find a reference, manage household records, or begin a learning session. Keep only destinations that support those activities. The page earns its place when it shortens a real route you use.

Organize by the action you want to take

Use labels such as “Continue current project,” “Find technical references,” or “Review saved reading.” A list organized only by company names requires you to remember which company serves the task. Add a short explanation when a destination's purpose is not obvious.

Separate stable resources from temporary work. A documentation homepage may remain useful for months, while an active project link may change next week. Give temporary links a review date or an obvious home in an active-work section. Otherwise the page gradually turns into another archive you hesitate to edit.

Limit the first screen to the paths you use most often. A longer reference section can sit below it. Avoid measuring success by the number of links collected. If two destinations answer the same need, explain the distinction or choose one as the default.

Choose the simplest maintainable format

A bookmarked document, a private note, or a static HTML page can all work. Choose based on access, editing effort, and whether you need the page offline. A custom application adds maintenance that a list of links may not need.

MDN's introductory HTML guidance explains headings, paragraphs, lists, and links. Those basic elements are enough for a useful starting page. You do not need a dashboard framework, embedded analytics, or a live widget for every destination.

Current work
  Project brief — authoritative scope and next milestone
  Task board — unfinished work and owners
Reference
  Language documentation — version-specific API behavior
  Research inbox — material awaiting evaluation
Review
  Broken or uncertain links — resolve before reuse

This outline is an example of content organization, not an interface requirement. Use your own vocabulary. If you share the page, choose labels that another person can understand without learning your private abbreviations.

Make navigation understandable

Use meaningful link text. “Renew household insurance” is more useful than “click here,” provided that is genuinely what the destination supports. Distinguish an official account portal from a comparison article or a personal note about the same subject.

W3C WAI's heading guidance recommends headings that reflect the organization of a page. Keep a logical hierarchy so the sections are understandable when scanned or navigated with assistive technology. Do not choose heading levels merely for their default visual size.

Check the page on the device where you will use it. Links should be easy to activate, long labels should wrap, and the reading order should remain sensible. Avoid making essential navigation depend on hover, color, or a decorative image.

Keep private information out of public routes

Decide whether the page is private before adding destinations. A link may contain a sharing token, a private document identifier, or a temporary sign-in parameter. Use a stable entry point instead of saving a sensitive one-time URL. Never place passwords or recovery codes on the page.

If you publish the page, inspect every destination as though a stranger could read it. Even an inaccessible link can reveal a project name or an organization relationship. Keep private operational links in an access-controlled location rather than relying on an obscure public address.

Bookmarks may already meet part of the need. Chrome's bookmark documentation describes creating, finding, editing, and organizing saved destinations. A start page should add useful context or task organization; it need not replace a bookmark system that already works.

Build and maintain the map

A hypothetical part-time learner

Hypothetical example: Amina studies programming after work. Her browser contains course pages, exercises, documentation, and interesting articles. She proposes a starting page with three immediate routes: continue the current lesson, open the exercise repository, and consult documentation for the language version used by the course.

She places optional reading below those routes and keeps account recovery material elsewhere. During a later review, she would remove links to completed course modules from the active section while preserving them in an archive if still useful. These are proposed organizing choices, not measured productivity results.

If Amina repeatedly leaves the page to search for the same missing resource, she adds that route. If she never uses a decorative widget, she removes it. Actual retrieval behavior guides the design more reliably than the desire to fill every space.

Start-page checklist

  • Does the first screen support your most common next actions?
  • Are destinations verified and labeled by purpose?
  • Are temporary links distinguishable from stable references?
  • Have sensitive tokens and private context been excluded from public copies?
  • Do headings and links work without visual decoration?
  • Can you edit the page without maintaining a separate application?

A start page cannot keep external resources accurate or prevent a destination from changing. Its useful promise is smaller: you know why each route is present, where it leads, and when it needs review. Keep that promise easy to maintain.
excerpt: Build a small personal web starting page around repeated tasks, verified links, clear labels, and a privacy boundary you can maintain.
seoTitle: How to Build a Personal “Start Here” Page for the Web
seoDescription: Create a useful personal start page with task-based links, accessible headings, private-link checks, and a simple review process that keeps it relevant.

sourceNotes.claims: Basic semantic HTML headings, lists and hyperlinks.
Logical heading organization for accessible navigation.

No text, letters, numbers, logos, watermarks, code, interfaces, or fake screenshots. Opaque background. Communicate the exact article topic visually.
